Entries.SourceTerm: 修心未到無心地，萬種千般逐水流

Senses.PreferredTarget: Until cultivating the mind reaches the ground of no-mind, countless things follow the current downstream
AlternateTargets: If the mind has not reached no-mind, myriad matters are swept along with the water
SearchAliases: not reached no mind countless things swept away
cultivating mind things follow the current
Senses.Note: The line contrasts an unfinished movement toward “no-mind” with the many things that continue to be carried by a current. Zhengjue Yi uses it at the close of a verse on a person with clear eyes who falls into a well. Yuanwu invokes it when pressing listeners beyond a neat comparison of case replies; Gulin gives it after warning against stopping short in the search for teachers. Pinjixiang ends a hall address with it. “No-mind” here means freedom from clinging and calculating, not unconsciousness or the abolition of ordinary awareness.

Senses.Note: Huairang answers the Sixth Patriarch that cultivation and realization are not absent, but defilement is not allowed. Tianyin cites this as a model of realized effort, Muyun brings it into an instruction on remaining unstained, and Shiyu compares it with Qingyuan's refusal of graded positions. Qingzhong revoices the pair for his own assembly. The two clauses check each other: neither mere achievement nor the denial of work is the answer.

Senses.Note: Asked by the Sixth Patriarch whether cultivation and realization are needed, Nanyue Huairang answers that they are not absent, but defilement cannot occur. Later teachers keep the two clauses together. Wanru annotates the exchange, Zizhou questions attachment to “unstained,” and Miyin argues that the line calls for care rather than carelessness. Foyuan responds with a verse, while Tianran asks what remains to cultivate if staining is impossible.

Senses.Explanation: One mighty roar, often pictured as a lion’s, stands for an answer or action with enough force to scatter lesser voices. Baiyu pictures everyone roaring like lion cubs, then warns that even this is still a point for a blow. Mi’an urges listeners to clear borrowed views and roar like lion kings. Poshan praises a novice whose single roar stills heaven and earth. Daxiu makes one roar split heaven and earth in a verse answering a question. Shipu imagines one roar breaking a world of foxes while urging the assembly to recognize a worthy teacher. Dahui compares the direct crossing of a river to a lion whose roar breaks the lesser beasts. Shitian calls for a young lion’s roar during the summer retreat.

Senses.Explanation: A deviation as fine as a hair can leave one a thousand miles off course. The second clause gives the scale of the consequence. Miyun throws down his staff to warn the assembly. Yune offers the pair as a direct answer on principle and event. Binya contrasts seeming alike with being the same. Fangrong strikes his staff to make the tiny error visible; Hanyu warns about a moment of hesitation. The full pair expresses the consequence that the shorter public clause leaves unstated.

Senses.PreferredTarget: All the manifold forms are stamped by one principle
AlternateTargets: The myriad forms of the world bear the seal of one reality
SearchAliases: myriad forms sealed by one principle
Senses.Note: The inherited line says the countless forms of the world bear the seal of one principle. Later masters put pressure on the word ‘one’: Baichi asks a laywoman whether it is inside or outside the forms, while Yikui asks what exactly counts as the principle. Baiyu gives a sweeping water image and then warns against resting in the explanation.

Senses.Explanation: ‘All the manifold forms are stamped by one principle’ is an inherited line about the relation of the many and the one. These masters use it to press listeners who imagine that the one principle might be found somewhere outside the forms before them. Baichi asks a laywoman whether the one principle is inside the myriad forms or outside them. Yingning quotes the ancestor's line and says that seeking Buddha outside mind misses what is already at hand. Hanyue starts a hall talk with the line, links visible forms to mind, and shouts. Baiyu gives a great-water image for diverse beings, then warns that a capable listener should wash his ears rather than settle on the explanation. Yikui raises the line at a birthday gathering, asks what should be called the one principle, and brings the question into the shared work of the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: The formula begins, “Before your eyes, there is no thing,” then says that its import is before the eyes, yet it is not a thing before the eyes and is not reached by ears or eyes. Senses.Explanation: Read the move and weigh the ounces names exact, responsive appraisal: seeing what an encounter calls for and measuring the response without excess or shortage. Mi'an Xianjie places it after 'raise one and clarify three' among the powers displayed in a formal hall address. Hongjue Min's questioner uses the pair to open a three-phrase interview, and Feiyin Tongrong makes it the capacity that joins ancient and present in one thought. Shiqi Tongyun says a patch-robed monk must possess it; Fushi Mingfang says the right person naturally does. Hansong Zhicao supplies the limit: even cutting off the ten directions while reading the move and weighing the ounces may still be driving a stake and washing one's feet against a bridge post.

Senses.Explanation: One beat of the newborn buddha's tableau — eyes sweeping the four quarters between the seven steps and the one finger to heaven — raised on the birthday not to honor it but to price it: Yunmen's blow waits at the end of nearly every telling. The raised tableau and its price: Poshan Haiming has old Sakyamuni walk out of Lady Maya's womb — seven steps, the eye-sweep, one finger up one down, sole-honored in heaven and on earth — and calls it a season for raising arms, before old thief Yunmen's blow; Yulin Tongxiu holds one must first have the buddha-ancestors' vast mind to live into that scene as Sakyamuni did, and only then to do as Yunmen did — strike him dead and feed him to the dog for the sake of peace under heaven; Koho Kennichi raises the same scene at the bath-buddha hall with Yunmen's line, ruling the Shaoyang old man toiled in vain; Chulin Shangrui sets it two thousand years on — born into Suddhodana's house on the fourth of the fourth, and even that does not step outside this very season. The verdicts on the sweep itself: Xuedou Chongxian tells the assembly to look at the first-awakened — not yet left Tusita, already descended; not yet out of the womb, the delivering of beings done — and even if you say seven steps and the eye-sweep, sole-honored between heaven and earth, still there are those who will not let him pass; Xiuye Minglin raises the scene and rules the World-Honored only knew advancing, not looking back; Zhongfeng Mingben verses it — ignorance filling the belly and evil wrapped round the body, barely out of the womb held in soft restraint, eyes sweeping the four quarters and seven steps round, not knowing how deep the mud and water underfoot; Yinyuan Longqi is asked straight — sole-honored set aside, explain the eye-sweep and the seven steps — and answers with the nostril half exposed.

Senses.Explanation: The lotus question — how is it when the lotus has not yet come out of the water? — answered at the root with the lotus itself and the leaf, paralleled by the Jingzhong elder's full pool of buds, and re-answered with stone turtles, mud-roots, cliff-side tea, and world-filling cold and heat from the Song case-desks to the Qing hermitages. The root sits in Zhimen Guangzuo's own exchange, carried in his record among the ancient venerables: asked how it is when the lotus has not yet come out of the water — the lotus; and after it emerges — the leaf; and then his own ruling: if one thing exists, Vairocana falls among the unenlightened; if the ten thousand things do not exist, Samantabhadra loses his field — right at such a moment, where does Manjusri come out from?; and if he cannot come out, the golden-maned lion's waist breaks; the Jingzhong elder's parallel answer, carried in Danxia Zichun's ode section: how is it when the lotus has not yet come out of the water — a pool running full of buds; and after it emerges — the leaves fall and no one knows autumn; and Danxia's ode over it: the white root not yet sprouted is no hidden truth, the red blossom at the water no claiming of the sun; travelers, send no message of it — a clear wind of itself carries the scent far; and Guxue Zhenzhe, at the Huangyan temple, raises the root case to the assembly — Zhimen answering thus truly cuts off the crowd's stream, yet examined closely, there is still a leaning on something — so today, were someone to ask this mountain monk how it is when the lotus has not yet come out of the water, he is told: the Kaiyuan stone turtle; and after it emerges: the Yangzhou red-crowned crane. Gusu Zun, in the recorded exchanges of his own record: asked how it is when the lotus has not yet come out of the water — the root is in the mud; after it emerges — the leaf roofs the clear waves; and both at once, out and not yet out — let go or gathered in, it is up to him; the monk bows — you have it; the monk starts to speak, and the blow falls; Kongyin Daodu, in the fireside talk of his own record, asked the same by the trainee Lingmi: how is it when the lotus has not yet come out of the water — under the cliff, brewing tea and burning leaves; and after it emerges — by the stream, flowing water scattering peach blossoms; and Yu'an Zhiji, carried in the Hidden Black Beans collection: asked how it is when the lotus has not yet come out of the water — cold, then cold through the whole of heaven and earth; and after it emerges — heat, then heat through the whole of heaven and earth.
